cover-01.title: TypeScript You MIGHT Like
cover-01.author: Bob Fornal
cover-01.bio1:
Entrepreneur
Code-squid provides solid, in-depth frontend training that is supported with real-world code projects. Blessed husband and proud father of two.
cover-01.bio2:
Microsoft MVP | Torc Ambassador |
Senior Solutions Developer II at Leading EDJE, Inc.
Passionate about learning, testing, mentoring, speaking, and personal growth.
cover-01.notes: I've had quite a few conversations over the years where the developers are polarized. About half LOVE TypeScript and the other half HATE it. The ones who hate it are usually fighting against the type system, writing tons of type annotations, and getting frustrated with the error messages. In this talk, I want to share some patterns and best practices that have helped me and my teams use TypeScript in a way that is actually enjoyable and beneficial. My goal is to show that TypeScript doesn't have to be painful, and that with the right approach, you MIGHT actually ... like it.

we-have-all-been-there.title: TypeScript: We've All Been There
we-have-all-been-there.text1:
The ongoing Horror Show ...
  • Async/Await Issues (Freddy Krueger's Promise Nightmare).
  • Circular Type References (The Hills Have Eyes: inbred mutations).
  • Conditional Types Gone Wrong (The Thing - shapeshifting horror).
  • Deeply Nested Object Access (Hereditary's ancestral curse).
  • Generic Type Inference Hell (Hellraiser's Cenobites).
  • Massive Instances (Godzilla - IDE destroyer).
  • Method Chaining with Complex Types (The Ring's 7-day curse).
  • Union Type Narrowing Failure (Get Out - the Sunken Place).
we-have-all-been-there.notes:
"TypeScript error message from hell"
"We've all been here. Let's fix that."
Key Message "TypeScript is a tool, not a religion. Use what helps, skip what doesn't."

introduction-what-we-will-cover.title: What We'll Cover
introduction-what-we-will-cover.text1:
1. Just Enough Types Philosophy.
  2. Patterns That Prevent Bugs.
  3. Features You're Probably Overlooking.
  4. Keeping Types Manageable.
  5. Real-World Patterns with TypeScript.
  6. Practical Tips & Tricks.
  7. Common Pitfalls to Avoid.
  8. Adoption Strategy.

01-01-just-enough-types.title: 1.1. Just Enough Types: Stop Fighting Inference

01-02-type-when-it-matters.title: 1.2. Just Enough Types: Type When It Matters
01-02-type-when-it-matters.notes: Function boundaries ARE the right place.

01-03-unknown-safety-net.title: 1.3. Just Enough Types: The "Unknown" Safety Net
01-03-unknown-safety-net.notes:
The "any" is an escape hatch.
Use "unknown" for safe type narrowing

part-one-summary.title: Part 1: Summary
part-one-summary.text1:
1. Just enough types: stop fighting inference.
  2. Type when it matters.
  3. The unknown safety net.

02-01-discriminated-unions.title: 2.1. Bug Pattern Prevention: Discriminated Unions
02-01-discriminated-unions.notes:
Boolean flag nightmare that kills unknown checks.
Make invalid states impossible.

02-03-readonly.title: 2.3. Readonly (stop accidental mutations)
02-03-readonly.notes:
Readonly is a powerful tool for immutability.
Readonly arrays and objects prevent accidental mutations.
Readonly also makes intent clear to other developers.

part-two-summary.title: Part 2: Summary
part-two-summary.text1:
1. Discriminated Unions prevent bug patterns.
  2. Literal Types are better than enums.
  3. Readonly stops accidental mutations (makes intent clear).

03-01-template-literal-types.title: 3.1. Template Literal Types (type-safe routes)
03-01-template-literal-types.notes:
Stop strongly-typed code.
Template literal types = safety + autocomplete for strings.

03-02-index-signatures-with-constraints.title: 3.2. Index Signatures with Constraints (type-safe dictionaries)
03-02-index-signatures-with-constraints.notes:
Type-safe dictionaries.
Index signatures with constraints = safety + autocomplete for object keys.

03-03-satisfies-operator.title: 3.3. Satisfies Operator (type-safe objects)
03-03-satisfies-operator.notes:
Type-safe objects.
Satisfies operator = safety + autocomplete for object values.

03-04-non-nullable-and-utility-types.title: 3.4. NonNullable and Utility Types (stop null/undefined bugs)
03-04-non-nullable-and-utility-types.notes:
Stop null/undefined bugs.
NonNullable and utility types = safety + intent clarity for null/undefined.

part-three-summary.title: Part 3: Summary
part-three-summary.text1:
1. Template Literal Types for type-safe strings.
  2. Index Signatures with Constraints for type-safe dictionaries.
  3. Satisfies Operator for type-safe objects.
  4. NonNullable and Utility Types to stop null/undefined bugs.

04-01-dry-derive-types.title: 4.1. DRY Derive Types with "Omit," "Partial," and "Pick"
04-01-dry-derive-types.notes:
DRY Derive Types with "Omit," "Partial," and "Pick".
Use "Omit," "Partial," and "Pick" to avoid repetition and keep types in sync.

04-02-typeof-and-keyof.title: 4.2. Let Code Generate Types ("typeof" and "keyof")
04-02-typeof-and-keyof.notes:
Let code generate types with "typeof" and "keyof".
Use "typeof" and "keyof" to create types based on existing values and keys.

part-four-summary.title: Part 4: Summary
part-four-summary.text1:
1. DRY Derive Types with Omit, Partial, and Pick.
  2. Let Code Generate Types with typeof and keyof.

05-01-type-safe-event-emitters.title: 5.1. Type-Safe Event Emitters
05-01-type-safe-event-emitters.notes:
Type-safe event emitters.
Use generics and mapped types to create type-safe event emitters.

05-02-builder-pattern-with-type-state.title: 5.2. Builder Pattern with Type State
05-02-builder-pattern-with-type-state.notes:
Builder pattern with type state.
Use generics and conditional types to create a builder pattern that enforces correct method chaining.

05-03-type-safe-dependency-injection.title: 5.3. Type-Safe Dependency Injection
05-03-type-safe-dependency-injection.notes:
Type-safe dependency injection.
Use interfaces and generics to create a type-safe dependency injection system.

part-five-summary.title: Part 5: Summary
part-five-summary.text1:
1. Type-Safe Event Emitters.
  2. Builder Pattern with Type State.
  3. Type-Safe Dependency Injection.

06-01-exhaustive-switch-checks.title: 6.1. Exhaustive Switch Checks
06-01-exhaustive-switch-checks.notes:
Exhaustive switch checks.
Use discriminated unions and the never type to ensure all cases are handled in switch statements.

06-02-branded-types.title: 6.2. Branded Types (Prevent Mixing Similar Types)
06-02-branded-types.notes:
Branded types.
Use branded types to create nominal types for added type safety.

06-03-assert-functions.title: 6.3. Assert Functions
06-03-assert-functions.notes:
Assert functions (custom type guards).
Use assert functions to create custom type guards for complex type checks.

06-04-type-predicates-for-array-filterin.title: 6.4. Type Predicates for Array Filtering
06-04-type-predicates-for-array-filterin.notes:
Type predicates for array filtering.
Use type predicates to create type-safe array filters that narrow types.

part-six-summary.title: Part 6: Summary
part-six-summary.text1:
1. Exhaustive Switch Checks with discriminated unions and the never type.
  2. Branded Types to prevent mixing similar types.
  3. Assert Functions (custom type guards) for complex type checks.
  4. Type Predicates for Array Filtering to create type-safe array filters.

07-01-do-not-abuse-generics.title: 7.1. Do NOT Abuse Generics
07-01-do-not-abuse-generics.notes:
Generics are powerful, but they can be overused.
Don't use generics when a specific type is sufficient.

07-02-avoid-type-assertions.title: 7.2. Avoid Type Assertions (unless necessary)
07-02-avoid-type-assertions.notes:
Type assertions ("as") can be a sign of a design problem.
Avoid type assertions by improving your types or using "unknown" for safe narrowing.

07-03-do-not-fight-the-compiler.title: 7.3. Do NOT Fight the Compiler
07-03-do-not-fight-the-compiler.notes:
Don't fight the compiler.
Embrace TypeScript's type system and let it guide your code design for better safety and maintainability.

part-seven-summary.title: Part 7: Summary
part-seven-summary.text1:
1. Do NOT Abuse Generics.
  2. Avoid Type Assertions (unless necessary).
  3. Do NOT Fight the Compiler.

08-01-start-small.title: 8.1. Start Small: Incremental Adoption
08-01-start-small.notes:
Start small with incremental adoption.
Introduce TypeScript gradually to your codebase, starting with new files or modules.

08-02-the-80-20-rule.title: 8.2. The 80/20 Rule
08-02-the-80-20-rule.text1:
Focus on high-value areas first:
  1. API boundaries (requests/responses).
  2. Shared utility functions.
  3. State management.
  4. Configuration objects.
Skip (for now):
  • One-off scripts.
  • Legacy code you rarely touch.
  • Over-typed utility functions.
08-02-the-80-20-rule.notes:
The 80/20 rule: focus on high-impact areas.
Focus on high-value areas first:
  1. API boundaries (requests/responses)
  2. Shared utility functions
  3. State management
  4. Configuration objects
Skip (for now):

  • Legacy code you rarely touch
  • Over-typed utility functions

part-eight-summary.title: Part 8: Summary
part-eight-summary.text1:
1. Start small with incremental adoption.
  2. Focus on high-value areas first (80/20 rule).

quick-wins-you-can-apply-today.title: Quick Wins You Can Apply Today
quick-wins-you-can-apply-today.notes:
• Literal types for constants
  • Readonly for immutability
  • satisfies for safe configuration
  • Type predicates for filtering
  • Exhaustive checks

key-takeaways.title: Key Takeaways
key-takeaways.text1:
1. Type at boundaries, infer in the middle.
  2. Make invalid states unrepresentable (discriminated unions).
  3. Derive types from single sources (DRY principle).
  4. Use unknown, not any.
  5. TypeScript is a tool, not a test of purity.

resources-for-further-learning.notes:
• TypeScript doesn't have to be painful.
  • These patterns have saved hours of debugging, prevented production bugs, and made the code easier to refactor.
  • Pick one or two that resonate with you, try them, and see if TypeScript becomes something you MIGHT actually ... like.
